headline: WMO Says El Niño Will Become Very Strong, Persisting Into Early 2027
seoTitle: WMO: El Niño to Become Very Strong Into 2027 | FMB News
seoDescription: The World Meteorological Organization says El Niño is expected to strengthen to very strong intensity and has a nearly 100% likelihood of persisting through February 2027.
deck: The global weather agency now sees near-certain persistence through February 2027, strengthening the case for Philippine preparation for drought, heat and water stress even while Habagat can still bring destructive rain.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The World Meteorological Organization said El Niño is firmly established and is expected to intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with a nearly 100% likelihood of persisting through February 2027.

WMO said exceptionally warm conditions across the tropical Pacific support further strengthening before the event peaks toward the end of 2026. The agency warned that a very strong El Niño can shift rainfall and temperature patterns and raise the risk of drought, flooding and extreme heat in different parts of the world.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: PAGASA declared El Niño conditions present in the tropical Pacific on June 9 and said the pattern generally increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall, dry spells and drought across much of the Philippines. It also stressed that western parts of the country can still receive above-normal rainfall during the Southwest Monsoon, especially when tropical cyclones enhance Habagat.

By August 26, PAGASA was already describing the event as moderate-to-strong and expecting further strengthening. The new WMO assessment materially raises the global confidence and severity outlook: the event is now expected to reach very strong intensity, with near-certain persistence through February 2027.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: For the Philippines, a stronger and longer-lasting El Niño can increase pressure on agriculture, irrigation, water supply, hydropower and heat-sensitive communities. The risk does not mean every part of the country will be dry at the same time, and it does not remove the threat of intense monsoon or cyclone rainfall.
That combination matters for planning: communities can face damaging floods in the near term while still needing to prepare for reduced rainfall and water stress later in the season.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch PAGASA's next ENSO and seasonal climate updates for Philippine-specific rainfall, temperature, dry-spell and drought projections. WMO's global outlook does not replace local forecasts, and impacts will vary by region and month.

Key indicators for households and local governments include reservoir levels, agricultural drought assessments, heat advisories and any changes in PAGASA's rainfall outlook for late 2026 and early 2027.

importantDates: June 9, 2026: PAGASA declared El Niño conditions present in the tropical Pacific
August 26, 2026: FMB reported PAGASA’s moderate-to-strong El Niño outlook
September 3, 2026: WMO said El Niño is expected to become very strong and persist through February 2027
February 2027: end of WMO’s near-100% persistence forecast window
audit.socialCaption: WMO now expects El Niño to strengthen into a very strong event, with a nearly 100% likelihood of persisting through February 2027. For the Philippines, that raises longer-term drought, heat and water-supply risks even while Habagat and tropical cyclones can still bring damaging rain.
verificationNotes: The central forecast was verified directly against WMO’s September 3 press release and El Niño/La Niña update.
Reuters independently corroborated WMO’s assessment and reported the possibility that the event could become exceptionally strong; FMB does not state that it is already the strongest on record.
Philippine relevance was checked against PAGASA’s June 9 El Niño Advisory, which confirms El Niño conditions and explains the country’s below-normal rainfall, drought and Habagat-rainfall risks.
This is a material continuation of FMB’s August 26 climate coverage because WMO has raised the expected intensity to very strong and the persistence probability to nearly 100% through February 2027.

The continuation points to the earliest accessible canonical FMB reader page containing the August 26 El Niño report. The later standalone archive JSON is preserved but is not mirrored in the live CMS.
